analysis.one_liner: Requires pharmacy benefit managers to disclose drug prices, rebates, and their own profits to Medicare drug plans.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill requiring pharmacy benefit managers to report drug pricing and rebate details to Medicare drug plans died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are the middlemen that negotiate drug prices and decide which drugs are covered for Medicare drug plans. This bill would force PBMs to hand their Medicare plan clients an annual, itemized accounting: every drug dispensed, what the plan and patients paid, how much of the manufacturer's rebate the PBM kept, how often prescriptions were steered to the PBM's own pharmacies, and why a brand-name drug was favored over a cheaper generic or biosimilar. Plans could audit PBMs, and PBMs would reimburse plans for penalties caused by their own failures. It would also order a Government Accountability Office study on overlapping reporting rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare drug plan sponsors and the tens of millions of people they cover, along with taxpayers, gain visibility into where prescription drug money actually goes — including revenue PBMs and their affiliates keep and how network pharmacy reimbursement compares with the PBM's own pharmacies. Independent pharmacies gain because the reports would expose gaps between what the PBM charges the plan and what it pays community pharmacies.

how_it_helps.text: PBMs must annually report to each plan sponsor an itemized list of drugs dispensed, total rebates and other manufacturer payments, and all revenue the PBM or its affiliates retained, in a standardized machine-readable format [S3].

PBMs with affiliated pharmacies must report what share of prescriptions went to their own pharmacies, the cost gap between affiliate and independent pharmacies, and any plan design that steers patients to affiliate mail or specialty pharmacies [S3].

Plans must be given written justifications when a brand-name drug or reference biologic is covered more favorably than cheaper generics or biosimilars, with estimated patient cost-sharing under each scenario [S3].
Plan sponsors get an annual right to audit the PBM, can choose the auditor, and PBMs must reimburse sponsors for civil penalties caused by the PBM's noncompliance [S3].
PBMs must define pricing guarantees transparently and disclose which drugs or price concessions were excluded from performance calculations, ending 'spread' math that hides true savings [S3].

analysis.who_pays: PBMs and their corporate affiliates bear the compliance cost of detailed annual reporting, audits, and potential penalties, and their opaque pricing practices would become visible to their plan clients and to federal watchdogs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their affiliates

drawbacks.text: The bill is transparency-only: it imposes no price caps, no ban on spread pricing, and no direct limit on what PBMs or their pharmacies can charge, so lower costs depend entirely on plans and regulators acting on the new data [S3].

Most disclosed information is confidential — the Secretary may not release it to the public in a way that identifies a specific PBM, plan, or drug price, so beneficiaries would see little of it directly [S3].

The bill's own GAO study requirement acknowledges that health plans and PBMs already face overlapping federal and state drug-price reporting rules; adding another annual report increases compliance burden, a burden the bill shifts onto PBMs but that could be passed through to plans and premiums [S3].
The requirements only begin with plan years starting on or after January 1, 2026, and enforcement runs through contract penalties rather than direct federal enforcement against PBMs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The compliance burden is real but narrow, aimed at the middlemen rather than at patients or pharmacies. The bigger weakness is design: it produces data for plans and regulators, not for the public, and it changes no pricing directly — so its value depends entirely on plans, CMS, and the Attorney General using the disclosures. It is a modest, well-targeted accountability step, not a fix for PBM-driven drug costs on its own.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto introduced the Medicare PBM Accountability Act on July 12, 2023, with Sens. Tillis, Wyden, and Crapo as original cosponsors, pairing the Senate Finance Committee's chair (Wyden) and ranking member (Crapo) on the same bill [S3, S1].

The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance that same day; the full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remainder of the 118th Congress [S5].
The bill had three cosponsors: two Senate Republicans and one Senate Democrat [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large pharmacy benefit managers, which avoided new disclosure, audit, and penalty obligations. Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers gained nothing from the bill's failure, since no alternative transparency requirement advanced through this bill.

for.name: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring PBM reporting and audits under Medicare Part D.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill, which was then referred to his own committee.

for.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor, giving the bill the support of both party leaders on the committee of jurisdiction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit manager industry
against.role: Industry lobby for the large PBM companies
against.what_they_did: The three dominant PBMs and their trade association ran a large lobbying campaign against PBM regulation during this period, which shaped how far PBM bills advanced in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's original cosponsors spanned both parties — the Senate Finance chair (D) and ranking member (R), plus one more Republican — and no vote was ever held to test whether that support held up.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (the large national PBMs and their affiliated pharmacies)
industries.note: The bill would require PBMs to disclose rebates, retained manufacturer revenue, affiliate pharmacy steering, reimbursement gaps, and generics they bury — data that directly threatens the opaque pricing practices at the center of their business. It does not ban those practices, but it arms plan sponsors and regulators to police them.

Reports on reimbursement gaps between the PBM's own pharmacies and independents, and on plans steering patients to mail-order affiliates, would give community pharmacies evidence in their disputes with PBMs.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D and Medicare Advantage plan sponsors
industries.note: Plans gain audit rights and detailed data on their PBM vendors, but must certify compliance annually and absorb new oversight obligations. Many large plan sponsors are affiliated with the same companies that own PBMs, which limits how hard they are likely to push.
